name: Freiwirtschaft
summary: Freiwirtschaft (free economy) is the market reform movement founded on Silvio Gesell's programme of Free-Land and Free-Money. It would put all land in public ownership and lease it by auction, with the rent paid to mothers by number of children, and it would charge holders of currency a carrying cost so money circulates and interest falls toward zero. Beyond that it keeps private enterprise, competition and free world trade, rejects Marxist nationalisation and centrally planned economies, and opposes tariffs, borders and nationalism.
scope: The classic Gesellian programme of Silvio Gesell's 'The Natural Economic Order' (Free-Land and Free-Money, 1916-1920), as described in the scholarship on the Free Economy movement (Preparata and Elliott 2004, Onken 2000) and the Historical Dictionary of Switzerland entry on the Freiwirtschaft movement. It covers the movement's core economic and land reform and its stated views on trade, borders and war. It excludes later revisions by followers, the movement's tactical dealings with the Nazi regime in 1933-34, and Keynes's critical discussion of Gesell. The preface's 1920s evolutionary and eugenic language is Gesell's own but is answered only where the statements ask about it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: The reform takes issue away from the banks and gives it to a public National Currency Office that issues and withdraws money (Part IV), the opposite of leaving money to the market.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Free-Money keeps money ('will not be abolished by Free-Money') and the reform is meant to raise the wage-fund, so neither money nor wages are to be abolished.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Gesell treats rented houses as ordinary capital whose rent falls toward the interest rate as building increases; he does not ban renting.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The reform is meant to enlarge the wage-fund and give workers the full product, not to end wage work.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Part II section 2: the State buys all private land, forests, building sites, mines and water-power, compensating the owners with securities.

arms-reduction.rationale: Gesell dismisses the 'foolish puppet-show of armaments, frontiers, tariff-barriers' as a product of dividing the earth; no level is specified.

ban-interest.rationale: Onken stresses that Gesell did not advocate outlawing interest as in the canonical prohibition, but removing its cause through carrying costs on money.

central-planning.rationale: Onken places Free Economy as a reaction against Marxist centrally planned economies, and Gesell argues that State control of economic life is the wrong course.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Gesell wants voluntary giving from the full product to flourish and fears the State making personal assistance superfluous, yet he also provides public mothers' payments and an unemployment insurance office.

collective-farming.rationale: Land is leased in lots sized to cultivators' needs, mostly to families, with large tracts for communist or cooperative colonies only as one option among many.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Onken records Gesell's advocacy of an open world market without capitalist monopolies, customs frontiers, protectionism and colonial conquest.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Competition between individuals is central to Gesell's idea of ascent, though he condemns conflict between nations as futile.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Gesell says the choice is between his competitive order and community of property, and he chooses competition.

delink-world-market.rationale: Gesell wants an open world market with no import or export barriers for all countries.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Gesell rejects Marx's remedy of political supremacy of the dispossessed through organisation and forcible expropriation.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The Natural Economic Order assures everyone the full proceeds of his own labour to dispose of as he sees fit; nobody requires sharing.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Gesell wants the earth treated as a globe with no import or export and no tariff boundaries, with national borders only administrative.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Gesell grants all men equal rights to the earth without distinction of race, religion, culture or bodily constitution.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Competition on equal equipment lets the leadership fall to the fittest; Gesell aims at equal starting conditions, not equal results.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Onken records that Gesell rejected 'Blut und Boden' ideas and held that all should settle anywhere regardless of birthplace, colour or religion.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Natives and foreigners must have the same right to the land and anyone on the globe may bid at the lease auctions; any nation restricting this is to be outlawed.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Part II section 1 lets large tracts go to communist, anarchist, social-democratic or religious colonies and cooperatives, so communities may try their own arrangements on leased land.

free-trade.rationale: Part II section 1 states that Free-Land 'also implies universal free-trade'; Onken adds his call for an open world market with global free trade.

free-trade-promotes-peace.rationale: Onken records Gesell's open world market without customs frontiers, protectionism or colonial conquest as a basis of peace among nations, in his lectures on gold, land and peace.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Gesell wants nature's selection through free competition and warns that State control of the economy would put human propagation under the State; he does not call for state limits on births.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Private ownership of land is abolished; land is leased by public auction to the highest bidder, not owned by whoever first works it.

human-decline-since-golden-age.rationale: Onken records that Gesell wrote 'The Ascent of the West' against Spengler's cultural pessimism and expected regeneration under the reformed order.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Part I ends by demanding that the whole product of labour go to the wage-fund 'with no deduction for rent and interest', ending unearned income.

labour-priority-over-capital.rationale: Gesell argues the reform shifts bargaining preponderance from capital to the dispossessed workers, who keep the whole product of their labour.

land-redistribution.rationale: Large estates are bought out with full compensation, but the land is leased by auction, not given to those who farm it.

land-use-tenure.rationale: The land belongs to the public and is leased by auction for a term; leases can be cancelled early by paying a fine, so individuals hold land by use not ownership, though leases are transferable.

land-value-tax.rationale: Gesell shares the aim of financing the state from land rent but rejects the tax route, following Flurscheim's public ownership and leasing rather than Henry George's tax that leaves private ownership.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Gesell calls his Natural Economic Order the 'Manchester System': once land and money privileges go, free competition without outside intervention does the allocating (Introduction).

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Onken records Gesell's rejection of anti-Semitic attacks on 'Jewish' usurers as a 'colossal injustice' and his distance from racist ideologies.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Gesell replaces gold-based money with managed paper Free-Money whose quantity is set by the Currency Office, and argues at length against the gold standard.

moral-incentives.rationale: The Natural Economic Order is founded on egoism, because only self-interest is strong enough to overcome indolence; Christian precepts must not be carried into economic life.

nation-first.rationale: Sovereignty over the earth rests with men, not nations, and Gesell calls for a voluntary European confederation and international cooperation.

national-resource-control.rationale: Part II section 1 says that 'English coal', 'German potash' and 'American oil' are only geographical terms: everyone on earth has the same right to them.

national-self-determination.rationale: Part II section 1: 'there are no rights of nations, no prerogatives of sovereignty, no rights of self-determination of States'.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Onken calls Free Economy a market economy without capitalism, an alternative beyond hitherto realized systems, set against both laissez-faire liberalism and centrally planned Marxism.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The whole programme aims to abolish every privilege that distorts competition, including those attached to land and to money.

no-central-bank.rationale: The reform replaces the banks of issue with a National Currency Office, a public monetary authority that is not a profit-making bank (Part IV).

open-borders.rationale: Part II section 1: everyone must be free to move wherever he wishes and enjoy the same land rights as natives; national boundaries become merely administrative.

paid-care-work.rationale: Part II and the preface pay the land rent monthly to mothers in proportion to their children as compensation for the burden of rearing them.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Onken reports that Gesell aimed to release mothers from economic dependence on working fathers and remove 'sex privileges'.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Onken records Gesell's call for a voluntary confederation of European states to promote international cooperation.

price-stability-first.rationale: Onken records that the carrying cost lets the money supply be adjusted so that the money unit has the same long-term stability as other weights and measures; stable prices are the aim of the monetary reform.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Onken records that Gesell located exploitation in the monetary system rather than in private ownership of the means of production; for him it is interest and rent that are unearned.

property-fundamental.rationale: Gesell abolishes private property in land (with full compensation) yet defends each worker's full product and private enterprise, so the record points both ways.

public-money-creation.rationale: Part IV gives a public National Currency Office the task of issuing money when the country needs it and withdrawing it when in excess, in place of private banks of issue.

public-ownership.rationale: Gesell rejects 'nationalisation or socialisation of production' as the communist answer; only land is taken into public hands and it is leased to private users (Introduction, Part II).

race-based-immigration-restrictions.rationale: Free-Land gives everyone an equal right to move and settle 'without distinction of race, religion, culture or bodily constitution'.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Gesell holds that all have an equal right to the earth without distinction of race and may settle wherever they choose.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Gesell demands freedom of movement and settlement for all and outlaws any restriction of it.

regional-resource-ownership.rationale: The earth belongs to all human beings equally, not to a nation or region; no group may retain privileges over land (Part II section 1).

residents-only-property.rationale: Free-Land makes freedom of movement and settlement real and denounces the closed communes that tie people to their place; any body restricting Free-Land is to be outlawed.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Part II section 1 gives everyone an equal right to the earth and sends the rent to the public treasury, with rent paid by the user of the land.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Free-Land gives everyone the right to settle anywhere and outlaws any nation, race or community restricting it.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Gesell founds the economic order on 'justified egoism' and holds that wise self-interest serves the whole; religion and law should protect those who obey it.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Part II section 1 says Free-Land implies universal free trade and complete elimination of all tariff boundaries; no nation may erect boundaries or levy import duties.

tax-holding-cash.rationale: The defining mechanism of Free-Money is a charge on holders: notes lose value weekly unless a stamp is attached, whatever the price level.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: In Weimar Gesell proposed a graduated wealth tax of up to 75 percent on large estates and big business to meet war costs, though it is a side proposal to his land and money reform.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Onken records Gesell's call to abandon expansionist politics, and the Natural Economic Order treats conquest as a useless result of dividing the earth.

war-builds-character.rationale: Gesell describes conquest as futile, with blood, sweat, corpses and treasures squandered in vain, and war as producing separation not union.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The only benefit Gesell designs, the land-rent payment to mothers, goes to all mothers including foreign ones living in the country, though he sets out no general welfare system.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Gesell holds women's freedom depends on the economic reform: paying them the land rent releases them from economic dependence on men.

women-suffrage.rationale: Gesell takes women's political vote for granted, calling it an 'empty boon' unless they also gain economic independence.

worker-ownership.rationale: Preparata and Elliott describe the Proudhon-Gesell strand as objecting to cooperative ownership of capital and holding to private possession of the means of production.

notes: Gesell's own text is the only full primary source; Keynes's chapter 23 was read but is a critic's and is not cited. Searched themes for more positions: government and democracy, women, religion, welfare and unions, taxation, immigration, war and colonies, trade, property and cooperatives. Gesell and his scholars say little on courts, policing, the environment, technology, speech, sexuality or religious law, so those stay null. The movement divided in 1924 between a moderate liberal Free Economy Federation and an anarchistic Physiocratic Task Force, which is why the state question is a split.
